references.text: Also describes the fat burned on the altar as 'food, a fire offering' to the Lord, the same expression as in 3:11
Refers to the sacrifices as 'the food of their God' (לֶחֶם אֱלֹהֵיהֶם), the same concept of sacrifice as God's bread/food
The priest presents 'your God's bread' (לֶחֶם אֱלֹהֶיךָ), a parallel expression for offerings
Refers to the fire offerings as 'the food of their God' (לֶחֶם אֱלֹהָיו)
Refers to the sacrifices from foreigners as 'their God's food' (לֶחֶם אֱלֹהֵיכֶם)
Describes the offering as 'my food for my fire offerings' (לַחְמִי לְאִשַּׁי), using the same terminology
The priest burns the offering on the altar as a fire offering with a pleasing aroma to the Lord, the same sacrificial act
The priest burns a grain offering on the altar as a fire offering to the Lord, a parallel sacrificial act
Ezekiel uses the expression 'my bread, fat and blood' (לַחְמִי חֵלֶב וָדָם) in connection with sacrifices
Malachi criticizes priests for presenting unclean food on God's altar, using the same concept of sacrifice as God's food
Lev 7:5 confirms that burning the fat as a 'fire offering' is a common liturgical pattern for both peace offerings and guilt offerings.
Lev 4:26 refers directly to the procedure in Lev 3 to define how fat should be burned in sin offerings.
Lev 4:35 assumes knowledge of the procedure in Lev 3 to carry out the burning of fat in sin offerings.
